newsitem.title: USA: Thai currency defense seen relying on attrition.
newsitem.headline: Thai currency defense seen relying on attrition.

text.p: The standoff between the Thai government and currency speculators is likely to extend over the next four to six weeks in a brutal war of attrition, U.S. trader and hedge fund managers said.

In the forward market, the Thai government stands to suffer heavy reserve losses if the baht is devalued before the large positions which it has put on to stem speculative pressure are closed, they said.

The Bank of Thailand has spent about $2 billion to $3 billion in interventions on the spot market, but its contingent liabilities in the forward market are several times larger, estimated a fund manager.
"We are half way through the crisis," he said. "I don't think the central bank would cave in at this point."

Most of the aggressive selling by international hedge funds in April and early May involved contracts over 60-day and 90-day baht forward rates, which eventually prompted the Thai government to impose a two-tier exchange rate system.

Hedge funds under the control of George Soros were reported to have $4 billion in forward currency contracts due in August, according to The Nation newspaper published in Thailand on Monday. A spokesman from Soros Funds in New York, citing company policy, declined comments on the report.

The pressure in the next 30 to 45 days is reflected in volatility of the baht forward rates. Traders quoted one-month rate at 86.8 percent of the spot bid and 96.6 offered. Two-month was bid 50 percent, six-month 31 percent and 12-month 24 percent.
In the latest round of baht selling on Finance Minister Amnuay's resignation last week, Thai corporations joined the fray and the battleground was mostly in the spot market, traders said.
David Rolley, a portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles in Boston, compared the situation to Mexican corporations selling pesos before the the devaluation in 1994.
"It was not just speculators who bet on an overvalued baht," he said, adding that "selling also came from legitimate corporate hedging against their dollar liabilities."
The Thai private sector owes $66 billion in foreign currency debt, of which the bulk is due in one year or less, he said.
Currnecy traders said concerted intervention by Southeast Asian central banks stablized the baht at about 25.00 per U.S. dollar and the level appeared to be holding.
The forward market, in contrast, was eerily slow, they said.
"The central bank has the upper hand right now," said a trader, noting that quite a few hedge funds were groaning because they were trapped in the market by the exchange control.
"It is the most vindictive system we have seen," said an analyst, who asked not to be named.

To be sure, hedge funds have mounted some unsuccessful currency attacks in the past, such as the assault on the French franc, but they could liquidate their positions in the open market and reclaim some value, whereas in Thailand's current two-tier exchange rate system, the speculators had no way out, he said.
"When it is over, I doubt anyone would ever try to attack the baht again," the analyst said.
